Power & Utilities.headline: Hydro-heavy, import-dependent electricity market; tight supply with ESCO/PPA-anchored pricing and limited exchange trading.
Power & Utilities.summary:
Georgia's electricity market is structurally hydro-dependent. The grid was supplied with 15.4 TWh in 2025 — 13.8 TWh of local generation plus 1.6 TWh of imports — with installed capacity of 4,675 MW (hydro 3,489 MW, thermal 1,154 MW, wind 20.7 MW, solar 10.8 MW). Hydropower accounts for roughly 71% of generation, which leaves the system seasonally vulnerable: Georgia is a net importer for most of the year except May–September, and was a net importer of about 1.0 TWh (US$24.3mn) in 2025.

Domestic consumption rose 3.5% y/y to 14.3 TWh in 2025, with direct (large industrial) consumers the fastest-growing group at +9.2%. Generation fell 3.0% y/y to 13.8 TWh on lower hydro (−3.4%) and thermal (−1.6%) output. Exports contracted sharply (−51.2% to 0.5 TWh; revenue −US$23.5mn) on weaker Turkish prices, while imports rose 26.9% to 1.6 TWh.

Pricing is anchored mainly by ESCO and long-term power-purchase agreements (PPAs) rather than a liquid spot market — only about 0.9% of supply traded on the GENEX exchange in 2025. The wholesale (balancing) price rose 4.1% y/y to 5.8 USc/kWh. The market is organized into generation (large hydro plus thermal and a small but growing renewables base), the ESCO/PPA offtake framework, and regulated distribution.

Power & Utilities.outlook:
Near-term fundamentals are tight. Demand grows roughly 3% per year (~0.6x GDP elasticity) while hydro-heavy supply additions have been modest, so import reliance looks structural rather than cyclical. Galt & Taggart's 2026 forecast sees consumption rising 4.6% to ~15.0 TWh and a continued net-import balance, with the balancing price edging up only ~0.8% to 5.9 USc/kWh — consistent with ESCO/PPA structures that have kept wholesale price growth near 0% CAGR over 2015-25.

New large-scale demand sources (data centres, EVs, crypto) are unlikely to move the system materially before 2035 — EV use was only ~0.3% of generation/imports in 2025. The medium-term balance of the market therefore hinges on the pace of new renewable capacity additions, hydrology, and whether the EU export-cable option advances.
Power & Utilities.caveats: Generation, consumption and trade figures are 2025 actuals (sourced to GNERC/ESCO via Galt & Taggart); 2026 figures are forecasts. TBC Capital's two Power reports are image-only PDFs and were not parsed for figures.

Auto & Auto Parts.headline: Georgia is a regional car re-export hub with no domestic production — large turnover, thin margins. Core market data is dated (2018-19).
Auto & Auto Parts.summary:
Georgia became a regional hub for the car trade through customs and trade-infrastructure reforms, turning into a car-exporting country without any domestic car production. Auto-business turnover grew at a 14.8% CAGR over 2010-18 to reach GEL 2.6bn in 2018 (+17.6% y/y), split across three sub-sectors: sale of automobiles (64.7%), auto parts (31.9%) and auto servicing (3.4%).

Cars are among Georgia's largest export and import categories. Car re-exports — the country's second-largest export category — stood at US$408.9mn in 2018 (up ~1.7x y/y), while car imports reached US$598.2mn (+25.4% y/y). Azerbaijan and Armenia together took ~71% of re-exports in 2018 (Azerbaijan top by value at 46.5%, Armenia top by quantity), with Ukraine and the UAE as growth markets.

Despite large turnover the sector is low-margin: net profit margin averaged 5.1% (2015-17), in line with the broader trade sector. Auto servicing is the most profitable sub-sector (~23% operating margin) versus auto parts (~7%) and auto sales (~4.5%). Government policy from 2017 (higher excise on older / right-hand-drive cars, lower excise on hybrids, mandatory technical inspection from 2018) drove a shift toward younger, left-hand-drive, more fuel-efficient vehicles and a Toyota/hybrid (notably Prius) boom.

Auto & Auto Parts.outlook:
On the latest quantified market read (Galt & Taggart, 2019), the sector was expected to keep growing on three pillars: continued strength in car re-exports (1Q19 exports +52.8% y/y), gradual renewal of the aged auto park, and rising household incomes plus more women drivers. Mandatory inspection was seen as boosting demand for newer cars, parts and repair services, and — alongside a shift to younger insured vehicles — supporting growth in car insurance (only ~5.7% of registered vehicles were insured in 2018).

This market view predates more recent disruptions — notably the 2022-onward surge in re-exports to Central Asia and Russia — so current dynamics likely differ materially. A newer TBC Capital report (“Georgian Automotive Industry”, Dec-2024) exists but is image-only and was not parsed; the quantified figures here should be treated as a 2018-2019 baseline rather than current data.

Tech & IT.headline: Georgia's fastest-growing sector since 2022: ICT now ~8% of GDP, IT exports up ~52% YoY, with e-commerce a fast-rising second leg.
Tech & IT.summary:
ICT — powered by IT services — has become one of Georgia's main growth engines. It has been the fastest-growing part of the economy since 2022 and is now the 4th-largest sector, at 8.2% of nominal GDP in 9M25. The sector is intensely export-oriented: ICT exports reached US$842mn in 2024 (10.9% of services exports) and surged 52.3% YoY to US$898mn in 9M25 (14.0% of services exports). IT-sector turnover hit GEL 4.5bn in 9M25 (+2.1x YoY), rebounding hard from a soft 2024, when exports dipped 9.2% on weaker prints from several large international providers (EPAM, Exadel, JettyCloud, Exactpro).

Growth is driven overwhelmingly by international companies and relocated specialists, drawn by Georgia's light tax regime (International Company Status: 5% CIT on distributed profit, 5% personal income tax, 0% dividend/property tax) plus low internet costs, cheap living and a favourable climate. Since the Russia-Ukraine war, individual IT professionals dominate — 93% of ~22,400 registered IT-service providers in Sep-25 are individual entrepreneurs. Average IT salaries have more than doubled since 2020 (GEL ~7,000/month, ~3.4x the wider business-sector average). Computer programming is now ~59% of ICT revenue (9M25), overtaking telecoms (~23%).

E-commerce is the other Tech & IT leg. Georgia's online market expanded roughly tenfold over 2018-24 to GEL 3.5bn and grew 40.6% YoY in 1H25; Galt & Taggart forecasts GEL 4.7bn for full-2025 and a 20.5% CAGR to GEL 10.7bn by 2030. Online shoppers reached ~1.0mn (37.4% of adults). Penetration is highest in fashion (15.6% of turnover in 1H25) and electronics (12.0%); cross-border purchases (Temu-led, China now ~48% of value) make up ~39% of the market.

ICT-services exports per capita (US$228 in 2024) remain far below regional peers and global leaders, framing large untapped export headroom.

For e-commerce, Galt & Taggart forecasts a 20.5% CAGR over 2024-30 to GEL 10.7bn, with retail penetration rising to ~13% (from 8.0% in 1H25), broadly tracking EU trends; goods are expected to rise to 63% of the online market by 2030 as the more mature services segment slows.

Education.headline: An ~GEL 3.3bn sector growing ~19% (2021-23); still government-led, with a fast-rising private segment and a higher-ed foreign-student boom.
Education.summary:
Georgia's education sector reached GEL 3.3bn in revenue in 2023, accelerating to an 18.7% CAGR over 2021-23 (from 10.7% over 2013-21). Government remains the main funder (~70.9% of sector revenue in 2023), but the private segment is gaining fast: private-sector revenue rose 25.5% YoY to GEL 958.2mn in 2023. Public education spending is 3.6% of GDP — below the EU's 5.0% average — and the government plans to lift it gradually toward 6% of GDP from 2028.

General (K-12) education revenue rose 15.5% YoY to GEL 1.5bn in 2023. Private schools enrol ~10.5% of pupils (66.5k in 2023/24), above regional peers (Turkey 7.4%, Armenia 2.9%) but below the EU's 16%, concentrated in Tbilisi, Batumi and Kutaisi. Private enrolment is expected to keep rising to ~73.1k by 2028/29 even as the total school-age population declines on falling fertility. Profitability is healthy but under pressure: private general-education operating margin was ~16.3% in 2023, with labour costs reaching ~70% of revenue (up from a 2017-21 average of 58.7%) — and a public-teacher pay rise (from Jul-2024) is expected to spill into private wages.

Higher education revenue rose 19.6% YoY to GEL 1.1bn in 2023, funded ~87% out-of-pocket. The standout driver is foreign students — Georgia's inbound mobility rate hit 17.3% in 2023 (one of the world's highest, near Switzerland's 19.1%), led by Indian students relocating after the Russia-Ukraine war (foreign-student CAGR 32.4% over 2021-23). 76.2% of foreign students attend private institutions, lifting private higher-ed operating margins to ~32.5% in 2023.

Education.outlook:
The market view is for continued double-digit sector-revenue growth, supported by strong government funding, rising household incomes and growing private-education demand. In general education, private enrolment is projected to climb to ~73.1k pupils by 2028/29 despite a shrinking pupil base — though profitability hinges on managing teacher-pay inflation, where larger, higher-scale schools are best placed to absorb cost pressure.

In higher education, Galt & Taggart projects Georgia could host 40-48k foreign students by 2028 (from ~30.7k in 2023), contributing an estimated US$420-500mn to the economy, with Indian demand and the planned shorter-degree structure as key levers. The defining medium-term tension across the sector is volume/demand strength set against rising labour-cost intensity at private operators.

Banks.headline: A concentrated banking market: Bank of Georgia and TBC hold ~75% of loans and deposits, with sector ROEs above 20%.
Banks.summary:
Georgia's banking sector is an oligopoly. Bank of Georgia and TBC together control roughly 75% of loans and deposits, with the #3 bank about six times smaller. The two leaders are listed in London via parent groups — Lion Finance Group (the renamed BGEO, parent of Bank of Georgia) and TBC Bank Group. Smaller players include Liberty, Basis Bank and Credo (the latter still largely a microfinance/agro lender, with loan yields around 24%). Both leaders have expanded internationally — Lion Finance via its 2024 acquisition of Armenia's Ameriabank (the #1 Armenian lender by loans) and TBC via a digital build-out in Uzbekistan (TBC UZ).

The sector accounts for an outsized share of the economy's profit pool: banking net profit was around GEL 3.3bn (~$1.2bn) in 2025, equivalent to roughly 4.0% of GDP — nearly twice the peer-market average. Structurally high net interest margins (~5% five-year average), mid-40s% cost/income, low cost of risk (~0.5%) and low NPLs (~2.5%) underpin ROEs above 20%. Deposits fund about 94% of loans, and the system has steadily de-dollarized, with the GEL share of loans up roughly 22 percentage points since 2015.

The loan book grew at about a 16% CAGR over 2015-25, outpacing nominal GDP by 4-5 percentage points, lifting the loan-to-GDP ratio from 46% to roughly 68%. In 1Q26 Lion Finance Group reported net profit of GEL 585m (+14% YoY) at a 27.4% ROAE, and TBC Bank Group reported GEL 365m (+15% YoY) at a 23.4% ROE.

Both leaders guide to a sustainable ROE above 20%, and the May 2026 NBG +25bp hike to 8.25% is incremental support to Georgian net interest margins.

The medium-term trajectory leans on continued financial deepening, growth in retail and consumer lending, and the maturing international franchises (Armenia and Uzbekistan), balanced against gradually moderating credit growth and rising real-estate exposure.

Insurance.headline: A small but fast-growing market — GWP ~GEL 1.06bn in 2023 (14% CAGR) — that is highly concentrated and profitable versus Europe.
Insurance.summary:
Georgia's insurance market wrote roughly GEL 1,064 mln in gross premiums in 2023, a 14% CAGR over 2019-2023, with a projected rise of about 18% to roughly GEL 1,256 mln in 2024. Premiums are dominated by two retail lines: health insurance (~42% of GWP, GEL 447 mln) and motor CASCO (~19%, GEL 205 mln), followed by property (~12%), life (~8%) and MTPL (~7%).

The market is highly concentrated — the seven largest of 18 operators write more than 80% of premiums, led by GPI Holding (17.3%), TBC Insurance (16.6%) and Aldagi (16.0%). Despite low penetration (~1.2% of GDP in 2022, versus a 1.0-11.2% range across European peers), profitability is strong: the industry combined ratio was 91.5% in 2023 (loss ratio 61.9% plus expense ratio 29.5%) and improved to about 89.3% in 3M 2024, well below the ~98-101% typical of European markets.

The two largest lines carry the highest loss ratios (health ~77%, CASCO ~78%), so margins depend on the business mix and on a steadily falling expense ratio, which declined about 2.5 percentage points over five years to 29.5% in 2023 despite wage inflation.

With a combined ratio well below European peers, the market is positioned to remain profitable as it scales.

The main swing factors are claims-inflation discipline in health and CASCO and any change to the state's role in healthcare; absent a universal-healthcare-style shock, the structural growth path remains intact.

Asset Management.headline: Nascent but fast-scaling capital markets — corporate bonds grew ~31% CAGR to ~GEL 2.1bn (2023); the wealth-management addressable market is put at ~GEL 13bn.
Asset Management.summary:
Georgia's capital market is young and bank-dominated but expanding rapidly. The local corporate bond market reached about GEL 2.1bn (~USD 800 mln) by end-2023, up from GEL 552 mln (~USD 205 mln) in 2018 — a ~31% CAGR (30.6% in USD) — with unique issuers rising from 5 to 11. Total issuances could approach roughly GEL 5bn over the following three years, and the local bond market could reach about GEL 5.4bn by 2026 as bonds become a more credible alternative to bank loans and deposits.

Wealth and asset management is even earlier-stage. The total addressable market is estimated at about GEL 13.2bn in 2023, roughly doubling to ~GEL 25.7bn by 2028 (~14.2% CAGR), against a thin revenue pool of around GEL 66m at a 0.5% fee assumption. The structural opportunity rests on under-diversified savings: Georgian households hold about 70% of wealth in deposits (versus 40-50% in Eastern Europe), and high-salary earners (above GEL 3.6k/month) grew roughly 4.7x to more than 100k over a decade.

The market is effectively a TBC Capital / Galt & Taggart (BoG) duopoly on the wealth-management and brokerage side and in bond underwriting. Equity-market liquidity on the Georgian Stock Exchange remains very low, and dollarization plus a narrow product range are the main structural constraints.

The local bond market could reach about GEL 5.4bn by 2026, with household securities holdings climbing toward a ~20% penetration rate within five years (from ~5.6%), tracking strong nominal GDP growth. The wealth- and asset-management addressable market is projected to roughly double to ~GEL 25.7bn by 2028, supported by capital-light, high-margin economics and a low domestic cost base.

Realizing this depends on widening the product set beyond short-dated bonds and deposits, deepening secondary-market liquidity, advancing the regulatory agenda (securitization, funds), and raising financial literacy — without which the gap between the large addressable market and the still-thin revenue pool will close only slowly.

Telecom.headline: A GEL 1.19bn telecom market led by mobile, with data as the growth engine while Pay-TV stagnates against streaming.
Telecom.summary:
Georgia's telecom sector generated GEL 1,193.7mn in revenue in 2022, split between retail (78.5%) and corporate (21.5%) and across mobile (GEL 696.2mn, 58.3%), fixed broadband (GEL 335.9mn, 28.1%), Pay-TV (GEL 135.8mn, 11.4%) and fixed voice (GEL 25.8mn). The market is a three-player mobile oligopoly — Magticom, Silknet and Cellfie — with Magticom leading on both subscribers (42% share) and revenue (49.3% share).

Mobile had 5.27mn subscribers in 2022 (about 143% penetration on GNCC methodology), lifted by migrant inflows and tourism recovery, with an additional 0.32mn signing up over 2022-1H23. Mobile data is the clear growth driver: traffic rose roughly 7x over 2019-1H23 on more subscribers and higher per-user usage, and ARPU has climbed since Comcom removed tariff regulation in July 2021. Fixed broadband reached 1.06mn subscribers in 1H23 (+6.4% y/y), boosted by real-estate sales and growing regional availability.

Pay-TV is the laggard — subscribers slipped 0.4% y/y in 1H23 (to about 698k) as Magticom dropped satellite TV and streaming services (Netflix, Setanta) gained, though revenue still grew modestly on higher tariffs and bundling. Total sector revenue rose 18.4% y/y to GEL 648.4mn in 1H23, mostly from mobile.

Fixed broadband subscribers should grow modestly, tracking real-estate sales and deeper regional and rural availability; globally, subscriber forecasts point to continued broadband expansion through 2030.

Pay-TV is expected to stay flat or decline further as streaming competition intensifies and more operators discontinue TV services in favor of their own or third-party platforms. Net-net, revenue growth should continue to lean on mobile (especially data) and, secondarily, on fixed broadband, while Pay-TV becomes a shrinking contributor.

Pharma.headline: USD ~2.4bn pharmacy-retail market, ~90% organized by revenue, consolidating toward a few large players; beauty/care and Armenia adjacent.
Pharma.summary:
Georgia's pharmacy-retail market is large and unusually consolidated for the region: roughly USD 2.4bn in size with about 8,000 pharmacy outlets, around 60% out-of-pocket spending, and approximately 90% of revenue already concentrated in organized (chain) operators. This contrasts with neighbouring Armenia, where only about 36.5% of stores are organized. The market structure spans three layers: core pharmacy retail, pharmaceutical distribution, and an adjacent beauty & personal-care segment.

The largest operator is Gepha (combining the GPC and Pharmadepot networks, roughly 433-439 stores), with an estimated 33-34% revenue share and around a 15% EBITDA margin. The next-largest players hold materially smaller shares. Consolidation is the defining dynamic: smaller chains such as Impex (around the 4th-largest, ~115 stores, lower revenue per store) and Pharm House (around the 6th-largest, ~53 stores, in financial restructuring) have been potential consolidation targets. A combination of the leader with these chains would lift the top operator toward roughly 40% revenue share and 46% store share, moving the market toward a triopoly structure. Both smaller chains run at roughly half the leader's revenue per store.

Two adjacent segments extend the sector. Beauty & personal care is a market of around GEL 1.1bn growing at roughly a 16.8% CAGR, served by prestige perfumery and cosmetics retailers (e.g. ICI Paris, Lutecia, Aromateque) with gross margins in the 40-55%+ range. Cross-border expansion into Armenia targets a roughly GEL 1.1bn market (about 1.4% of GDP) that is fragmented and wholesale-dominated, with the top-3 holding only ~26% share (Alfa the largest at ~13.1% by stores) — resembling Georgia 10-15 years earlier.

Healthcare Services.headline: Predominantly private, hospital-heavy system; private-sector revenue ~GEL 2.8bn in 2022, with DRG reform reshaping economics from 2023.
Healthcare Services.summary:
Georgia's healthcare sector is dominated by the private sector, which owns about 86% of hospitals — one of the highest rates of private hospital ownership among developed and emerging markets. The private sector generated GEL 2.8bn in revenue in 2022, roughly half of which came from the state Universal Healthcare (UHC) programme. After several years of margin deterioration, profitability rebounded in 2021 (boosted by COVID-19 management spending), with the EBITDA margin reaching 17.1% and the net profit margin 14.6%.

Demand is driven by an ageing population, improved accessibility, and a near-3x rise in public health spending to GEL 2.0bn over 2014-22, which cut out-of-pocket payments from 66% to 51% of total health expenditure (versus ~16% in the EU). The market is highly fragmented: the leading hospital chain Evex held roughly 13-17% share by hospitalizations/revenue, Aversi about 7%, and all other operators well below 3% each, leaving most of the market unconsolidated.

The system is structurally inefficient. Georgia has an oversupply of hospital beds (5.6 per 1,000 people in 2021, above peers and many high-income countries) against low bed occupancy (55% in 2021, far below the EU's 77%). It also has an oversupply of physicians (6.1 per 1,000, about 2x the OECD average) but a shortage of nurses (only ~1 nurse per physician versus 2-5 in Europe), and primary-care utilization remains low (4.0 outpatient contacts per person versus 7.0 in the EU).

The reform is expected to improve transparency and efficiency and foster healthier competition between hospitals.

The main counterweights are execution risks around DRG (quality of care and innovation if cost incentives are mispriced) and the system's entrenched inefficiencies — excess beds, low occupancy, and underdeveloped primary care that pushes patients directly to hospitals.

Retail - Grocery.headline: Georgia's largest consumer sector; modern grocery growing ~14-15% a year and consolidating around the 2024 Daily Group merger.
Retail - Grocery.summary:
Georgia's total FMCG/grocery market reached approximately GEL 22.7bn (incl. VAT) in 2024, growing 6.8% y/y, but the structural story is the shift to branded retail chains, which grew 14.9% to GEL 9.2bn and lifted their share from 37.6% (2023) to 40.4% (2024), on a trajectory toward roughly 52% by 2028. Within the narrower 'modern grocery' lens, the segment reached GEL 8.9bn in 2024 and is expected to exceed GEL 10.4bn in 2025 (~17% y/y). Modern penetration of about 40% still trails peer markets (~62-70%), leaving multi-year catch-up room. Growth has been volume-led: FMCG inflation collapsed from 15.9% (2022) to 0.8% (2024).

The market is consolidating. The 2024 Daily Group merger (combining Daily, Foodmart/Spar, Gvirila and Magniti) created the largest platform at about 27.5% of branded-chain revenue; top-5 concentration rose from 68.3% (2020) to 74.9% (2024). Discounters now hold roughly 49% of branded-chain revenue (up from 24% in 2018), while hypermarket/supermarket share fell from about 37% to 19%.

Profitability dispersion across operators is wide. A six-company peer set (FY24) spans premium operators (Agrohub: GEL 318m revenue, +25%, ~10.8% EBITDA margin) to hypermarkets in difficulty (Carrefour: GEL 789m, -2% y/y, operating loss, negative equity). Several profiled players carry negative equity (including the post-merger Daily Group, Goodwill and Carrefour). The vertically integrated incumbent Nikora reported around GEL 1.45bn revenue at roughly a 16.4% share.

The central case is roughly +8% total-sector CAGR over 2025-28 (to about GEL 30.8bn), with branded chains compounding at ~15% and modern grocery exceeding 55% of the total market by 2030 (~14% CAGR 2025-30). A consistent independent view sees +9.8% growth in 2025 (to GEL 24.2bn), moderating to ~5.9% in 2026.

The sector is bifurcating: premium and own-production operators and the vertically integrated incumbent show healthy returns, while hypermarket formats are under financial pressure. Further M&A consolidation is likely, with smaller chains and distressed assets as potential targets.

Retail - Apparel & Specialty.headline: Organized apparel roughly doubled in four years to ~GEL 1.4bn; tourist-led, with the top-5 holding ~63-75% of organized revenue.
Retail - Apparel & Specialty.summary:
Georgia's total apparel market roughly doubled from GEL 1.0bn (2020) to GEL 2.7bn (2024); the organized segment grew from GEL 472m to about GEL 1.42bn, up ~25% in real volume terms in 2024 (apparel inflation was -2.5%, so growth was volume-led). Organized share rose from 49% (2019) to about 52% (2024E), on a trajectory often compared to Bulgaria a decade earlier (~75% by 2034). Growth has been tourism-driven: 85-91% of incremental sector growth in 2023-24 came from visitors. The competitive structure is concentrated — the top-5 cohort holds roughly 63% of organized revenue in one model (cited as about 75% of the organized market), with high entry barriers (mall slots, franchise consent, working-capital intensity).

Peer economics (CY24) show a range of operators: RGG/Cenomi Georgia (Inditex master franchisee, ~59 stores) is the largest at GEL 357m revenue (+32%), with around a 15% adjusted EBITDA margin; Dressup (founder-owned, multi-brand) had the strongest unit economics — GEL 169m revenue (+31%), 52% gross margin, ~36% CAGR over six years; Waikiki (GEL 249m, +15%) saw margins compress in CY24 (gross margin from 43% to 26%, net loss). ICR Trade (footwear, GEL 97m, 50% gross margin) and TGL Sport (GEL 25m) round out the cohort. The largest player's Saudi parent, Cenomi, faced near-insolvency in 2024; Al-Futtaim acquired 49.95% in September 2025, and the Saudi CMA prosecuted 17 former insiders in May 2026.

Electronics & appliances retail (a separate specialty adjacency, 2022 data) is a roughly GEL 1.9bn import-driven market (about USD 583m in 2021), fragmented (top-10 ~50% share), with thin gross margins (~16% average) and ~4% EBITDA on a capital-light, lease-based model.

Electronics & appliances retail remains a slower-growing, fragmented adjacency (a 2021 forecast pointed to ~8.5% CAGR toward ~GEL 2.6bn), where value creation depends on consolidating to scale. _Macro & Cross-Sector.headline: Georgia macro: ~7.4-7.6% GDP growth in 2025E easing to 4.5-6.0% in 2026F, low single-digit inflation, falling debt, record FX reserves.
_Macro & Cross-Sector.summary:
This is the country-level macro backdrop underpinning all sectors, drawn from the year-end 2025 outlooks of two Georgian research houses (TBC Capital and Galt & Taggart). Georgia registered strong growth in 2025: TBC estimates 2025 real GDP growth at 7.4% and Galt & Taggart at 7.5% (with +7.6% recorded in 10M25). Growth was highly concentrated in information & communication (ICT) and education, which together accounted for almost half of 9M25 growth, and on the expenditure side it was consumption-led — consumption contributed over 100% of growth in Jan-Sep 2025, a third consecutive year. Nominal GDP reached roughly GEL 104bn (~US$ 38bn) in 2025E. Both houses expect growth to normalise in 2026 — TBC forecasts 4.5% and G&T 6.0%, with the medium-term potential rate seen around 5.5%.

The external sector was unusually strong in 2025. TBC reports the headline current-account deficit falling to a record-low 2.7% of GDP, with the underlying balance (excluding reinvestments) turning to a slight surplus — Georgia briefly a net creditor to the rest of the world for the first time on record — driven by surging ICT-services exports, rising money transfers (US$ 3.3bn in 11M25, +7.6% y/y) and tourism (~US$ 4.4-4.6bn, ~5.5mn arrivals). On G&T's wider definition (goods and services), the current-account deficit was ~5.0% of GDP in 2025E. The GEL strengthened ~4.1% YTD in 2025 on global USD weakness, higher FX inflows and de-dollarisation; rather than let it appreciate further, the NBG purchased about US$ 2.5bn, lifting gross international reserves to a record ~US$ 5.8-6.2bn. Both houses see the GEL broadly stable into end-2026, around 2.70-2.79 per USD.

Inflation re-accelerated modestly through 2025 (4.8% y/y by Nov-25, led by food and health) but is expected to ease: average annual inflation was ~3.9% in 2025E, with TBC forecasting 3.5% and G&T 3.0% for 2026, opening room for a ~50bp NBG policy-rate cut from 8.0% to 7.5%. Public finances were sound — fiscal deficit ~2.5% of GDP and government debt declining to ~34% of GDP (from 49% in 2021). Bank credit grew ~14.7% in 2025E and migration is proving sticky (67% of surveyed migrants intend to stay long-term, over 60% working in ICT).

risks: Russia-Ukraine conflict resolution — TBC flags this as its single most important variable (estimated ~40% probability) that could unwind migration, transit and trade tailwinds; TBC judges the net impact on Georgia negative, contrary to the mainstream view.

_Macro & Cross-Sector.outlook:
Both research houses expect growth to normalise from cyclical highs while remaining solid, but they differ on the magnitude. TBC's baseline is 4.5% growth in 2026 (incorporating some probability of a Ukraine conflict resolution, which it treats as a net negative for Georgia), with inflation averaging 3.5%, the policy rate easing to 7.5%, the headline current-account deficit widening to around 4.5% and the GEL drifting modestly weaker to ~2.79/USD as reserve-accumulation pressures fade. Galt & Taggart is more constructive — 6.0% growth in 2026 toward a ~5.5% medium-term potential, 3.0% inflation, a 50bp rate cut, a current-account deficit below 5% of GDP, and a broadly stable GEL (~2.70/USD, ~3.13/EUR), with scope for mild appreciation if the NBG accumulates less FX than in 2025.

The shared backdrop for sector pages is: low single-digit inflation, falling public debt (~34% of GDP), record FX reserves, a stable-to-firm GEL, robust tourism (~US$ 4.9bn forecast in 2026) and continued ~12-14% bank-credit growth. The two main two-sided swing factors flagged across both houses are the resolution of the Ukraine war and the durability of war-era inflows, plus domestic political and geopolitical uncertainty.

Real Estate Development.headline: Tbilisi and Batumi residential markets held up in 2024: prices rose ~11-12% while sales volumes flattened or eased.
Real Estate Development.summary:
Georgia's residential development market is concentrated in its two largest urban centres, Tbilisi and Batumi, and splits into a primary market (new units sold directly by construction companies/developers) and a secondary (turn-key) market. In 2024, Tbilisi's market stayed resilient: total apartment sales edged up 1.0% y/y to 40,346 units (primary 20,139; secondary 20,207), the average primary-market price rose 11.6% y/y to US$1,320/m2 (with the pace of growth slowing), and total market value reached US$3,132mn (+7.1% y/y). Rents softened to ~US$9.7/m2 (-9% y/y) while rental yield held near 8.8%, among the higher levels for regional peer cities. Construction permits eased 6.7% y/y to 1.8mn m2 of living area after a record 2023. Locals account for ~80% of Tbilisi buyers; the Russian buyer share fell to 2% (from 6%) as Israeli buyers rose to 10%.

Batumi cooled after the record 2022-23 boom. Registered sales fell 3.6% y/y to 15,195 apartments (primary 8,608; secondary 6,587), and developer-surveyed primary sales dropped 42.7% y/y amid political instability, migrant outflow and limited soon-to-complete supply. Prices still rose 11.4% y/y to US$1,470/m2 and market value reached US$977.5mn (+4.1% y/y), with rental yield around 8.8%. The local buyer share fell to 16%, with Russians at 18% and Israelis at 10%.

The market is fragmented across many developers (a Galt & Taggart survey in January 2025 tracked 17 systematic developers running 85 residential projects in Tbilisi). Both cities show decelerating price growth, a shift toward turn-key (secondary) apartments amid uncertainty, and construction costs driven mainly by wages (+23.7% in 2024). Much primary-market activity is financed through developer-offered inner-instalment schemes as mortgage rates remain elevated.

Galt & Taggart's view points to softer 2025 demand, with prices likely stabilising near current levels rather than continuing the double-digit climb. In Tbilisi, a projected economic slowdown, GEL depreciation and potentially lower rental yields are the key swing factors; in Batumi, prices are expected to hold while rental yields gradually ease unless tourist-driven rental demand rises materially.

The market enters 2025 from a position of relative strength — elevated (if decelerating) prices, high yields and a buyer base anchored by locals and developer financing — but political uncertainty and Batumi's supply pipeline are the dominant near-term swing factors.

Construction.headline: Construction is ~8.4% of Georgia's GDP; the linked materials & home-improvement market reached US$5.7bn in 2024, growing ~19% a year.
Construction.summary:
Construction is one of Georgia's largest economic sectors, contributing about 8.4% of GDP in 2024 — the highest share in the region — after holding in an 8-10% band over 2015-24. Activity is fed by both public infrastructure investment (public capex of GEL 7.9bn, ~8.7% of GDP in 2024, above the 4-7% typical of developing peers) and private residential/non-residential building.

The closely linked construction-materials and home-improvement sector reached US$5.7bn of revenue in 2024, growing at a 19.2% CAGR over 2020-24. It splits into construction materials (heavyside, US$2.1bn) and home improvement (lightside, US$3.6bn — renovation materials US$2.5bn, household appliances US$0.6bn, furniture & lighting US$0.5bn). Construction materials are mostly produced locally (67% local), while home improvement is import-heavy: roughly two-thirds of total sector revenue is imported goods, sourced mainly from Turkey and China (>50% combined).

Demand has been propelled by record construction-permit issuance (peaking at 12.0mn sq.m in 2024, +11.9% y/y into 1Q25), high government capex and a post-pandemic surge in apartment sales in Tbilisi and Batumi. Cement, concrete and rebar prices all rose sharply from 2021 on higher clinker, coal and steel input costs. Domestic rebar production share fell from 74.7% (2021) to 43.5% (2024) as imports gained ground, prompting a temporary import tariff in 2025.

Heavyside construction-materials demand should track the project pipeline, while home-improvement demand is supported by ongoing primary-market apartment sales. Price pressure eased somewhat in 2025 as the Red Sea freight spike receded and global steel prices stabilised, though rebar dynamics hinge on whether import tariffs are extended.

Industrial Goods.headline: Georgia's cement market reached GEL 749m in 2024 on the construction boom; the market is concentrated, with one integrated producer leading.
Industrial Goods.summary:
The Industrial Goods coverage centres on cement, a key Georgian building material, with the adjacent ready-mix concrete market. Cement consumption volume grew at a 7.6% CAGR over 2018-24, while consumption value reached GEL 749m in 2024 (17.0% CAGR 2018-24), outpacing real GDP growth (12.2% CAGR) and lifting the industry's GDP penetration. Value growth was driven by cement prices rising at an 8.7% CAGR (in GEL) on higher energy, clinker and labour costs. Imports are marginal (~6% of consumption volume); clinker, the main raw input, is imported (mainly from Azerbaijan, plus Turkey) with import value reaching US$80.1m in 2024. The closely linked concrete market reached GEL 894m in 2024 (18.2% CAGR), with concrete prices rising at a 9.5% CAGR.

The market is concentrated. Hunnewell Cement (formerly HeidelbergCement Georgia, rebranded August 2024) is the market leader at roughly 55-64% share and is the only fully integrated producer (clinker + cement + ready-mix concrete, ~2Mt installed capacity), with full-cycle plants at Kaspi, Rustavi and Poti and a network of concrete batching plants across Georgia. The second-tier players are much smaller: Kavkaz Cement (~6-8%, operating with a Lafarge license), Georgian Concrete Company, German Cement, GIA 2019 and Leader Beton, plus regional and import-based suppliers. Reported producer revenues for 2023 ranged from Hunnewell's GEL 564.7m down to GEL 16-90m for the smaller players.

Georgia already shows relatively high cement consumption per capita (882kg vs a ~696kg peer average for its income range). As a 'developing-stage' economy (GDP per capita in the ~US$5,000-30,000 band, the range where per-capita cement use typically rises), consumption per capita is expected to keep climbing alongside construction and infrastructure activity.

Logistics & Transport.headline: Logistics is a stable ~5.5-6.6% of GDP; freight turnover is projected to grow ~5.5%/yr and warehousing ~9%, with the Middle Corridor a key transit theme.
Logistics & Transport.summary:
Logistics is structurally important for Georgia given its position on east-west trade routes, holding a stable ~5.5-6.6% share of GDP over the past decade. Freight turnover (excluding domestic transport) grew at a 5.0% CAGR over 2015-24 (reaching ~37.7mn tons) and is projected to expand at a 5.5% CAGR through 2028, driven by domestic demand, export growth and rising Central Asian trade flows. Railway, road and maritime each carry roughly a third of international freight. Georgia ranks 79th of 123 on the World Bank's 2023 Logistics Performance Index, with infrastructure flagged as its main weakness.

The Middle Corridor (China-Kazakhstan-Caspian-Azerbaijan-Georgia-Turkey-Europe) accounts for about a quarter of Georgia's transit demand — 4.3mn tons in 2024, projected to reach ~9.7mn tons by 2030 as corridor economies develop. It is costlier and slower than the Northern and Southern routes today (US$4,500-6,000 per 40-ft container, 18-23 days) but benefits from planned investment: the Poti (>1mn TEU) and Anaklia (phase 1: 600k TEU) ports, plus railway modernisation lifting capacity to ~48mn tons.

On warehousing, Georgia has ~2.2mn m2 of total warehouse area; in Tbilisi supply reached ~920k sq.m in 2024 (+30% vs 2020), 94% dry / 6% cold, with a further ~33% increase expected by 2026. Dry-warehouse rents in new Tbilisi contracts nearly doubled, to ~US$5-6/sq.m in 2024 (class A: US$7-8). Warehouse demand is projected to grow ~9% a year over 2025-28, though rents are expected to stabilise. The market is unusually 1PL/2PL-driven — most companies own and self-manage warehouses, with 3PL (third-party logistics) outsourcing rare and driven mainly by international firms, particularly FMCG players.

Logistics & Transport.outlook:
Both transportation and warehousing are expected to keep growing steadily. Freight turnover is projected at a 5.5% CAGR through 2028, and by 2030 the economic development of Middle Corridor countries should bring the corridor close to full utilisation (~9.7mn tons), supported by the EU's Green Deal and Global Gateway agendas and rising Central Asian consumer markets.

Warehousing demand should grow ~9% a year over 2025-28, with supply transformation (replacing Soviet-era/Class C stock with modern, higher-quality warehouses) continuing for the next 7-8 years. Rents are expected to stabilise around current US$5-6/sq.m levels in the short term given increasing competition. The 3PL outsourcing model is unlikely to gain meaningful local traction in the medium term, as most Georgian companies prefer to own and self-manage warehouses.

Food & Beverage (FMCG).headline: Georgia's FMCG market reached GEL 22.7bn in 2024 (+6.8% y/y), with branded retail chains rapidly consolidating around a 2024 mega-merger.
Food & Beverage (FMCG).summary:
Georgia's FMCG market reached GEL 22.7bn (incl. VAT) in 2024, up 6.8% y/y, with growth driven by consumption volume rather than price. The defining structural trend is the rise of branded retail chains, whose revenue grew 14.9% y/y to GEL 9.2bn, lifting their share of the market from 37.6% to 40.4% over 2023-24. Expansion is increasingly regional: roughly 500 new stores opened in 2024 (about 350 in the regions), and regional chain revenue grew 23.6% y/y versus 9.3% in Tbilisi, which still accounts for about half the market (GEL 11.3bn).

The sector consolidated sharply in 2024. Several companies merged into Daily Group Holding (brands Spar, Ioli, Gvirila, Magniti), making it the market leader with a 27.5% share of branded-chain revenue and roughly 1,600 of about 4,000 chain stores. The top five chains hold 74.9% of branded-chain revenue. Discounters are the fastest-growing format (+24.2% y/y), in line with global trends and amplified by recent inflation.

Within food processing, beer is a notable sub-sector, with four large producers (Lomisi, Georgian Beer Company, Global Beer Georgia, Argo) and an estimated full-2023 turnover of about GEL 585mn (roughly 60% beer, 40% soft drinks). Meat and meat products generated about GEL 1.5bn in revenue in 2022 (primary GEL 930mn plus processed GEL 531mn), though the segment remains heavily household-based and lightly corporatized.

Food & Beverage (FMCG).outlook:
Galt & Taggart forecasts FMCG sector revenue to grow at an 8.0% average annual rate over 2025-28, reaching GEL 30.8bn by 2028, driven mainly by rising purchasing power. Branded retail chains are expected to outgrow other formats at a 15.0% CAGR and to push their market share past half the market to 52.0% by 2028 via geographic expansion, private-label development, e-commerce and data-driven personalization.

Structural headroom remains large: meat, dairy, and fruit & vegetables make up 39.1% of consumer FMCG spend but only 19.5% of branded-chain sales, pointing to untapped category potential. Vertical integration and private label (about 10% of sales versus more than 40% in parts of Europe, projected to reach about 20% by 2028) are widely cited as the key margin levers.

Wine & Spirits.headline: Georgia's wine & spirits sector posted GEL 1.43bn turnover in 2023: highly profitable, ~85% export-driven, but concentrated on Russia.
Wine & Spirits.summary:
Georgia is the historic 'cradle of wine,' with an 8,000-year history and more than 500 indigenous grape varieties. The wine and alcoholic-beverages sector recorded GEL 1.43bn in total turnover in 2023 (+4.6% y/y), having grown at roughly a 16% CAGR over the prior nine years. It is structurally export-dependent, with historically about 82-85% of revenue coming from exports, which makes it highly sensitive to external markets. In 2023 Georgia earned US$259mn from wine exports (4.1% of total goods exports) and shipped about 117mn bottles, an 11% volume decline offset by a higher average price (US$2.89/litre, +16% y/y). Russia accounted for 66% of wine export value in 2023.

The sector is among Georgia's most profitable. It posted a 30.2% gross and 20.8% operating margin in 2019 (1.4x and 1.7x the business-sector average), with the top-10 players sustaining roughly 41% gross and 25% EBITDA margins over 2017-20. It remains fragmented but consolidating: large companies rose from 12% of turnover in 2015 to about 41% in 2020. In 2023 there were 1,027 active wine producers and 118 spirits producers, of which only six wine and two spirits firms were classed as 'large.'

Brandy is a significant complement: Georgia was the 7th-largest brandy exporter globally in 2020 (US$113.2mn / 34.7mn litres) and a top supplier to Ukraine, Armenia, Russia and France. Production is concentrated in Kakheti (about 73% of vineyards and 79% of the grape harvest) and is climate-exposed; the 2023 harvest fell 23% y/y after hail and disease.

Wine & Spirits.outlook:
The market outlook is cautiously positive but hinges on diversification. TBC Capital projected sector turnover to grow about 5% in 2024, led by exports to Russia plus rising local consumption and tourism. Galt & Taggart's earlier base case saw wine exports nearly doubling toward about US$350mn by 2025, supported by vineyard investment, government backing, EU and China free-trade access, and rising average prices.

The central market theme is reducing Russia concentration: premium indigenous wines (Saperavi, Rkatsiteli, Qvevri styles) aimed at wealthier US, UK and Germany markets, and mass-market reds toward China. Continued consolidation, with large players gaining share, should improve the sector's financial resilience.

Agriculture.headline: Georgia's food-product market hit GEL 21.5bn in 2025 (doubled since 2019); gross agri output ~GEL 8.4bn, but low corporatization persists.
Agriculture.summary:
Georgia's food-product market reached GEL 21.5bn in 2025 (preliminary), roughly doubling over 2019-25, and is estimated to reach GEL 30bn by 2030. Local production supplies GEL 16.2bn, with imports at GEL 5.3bn and exports at GEL 4.5bn. Gross agricultural output was about GEL 8.4bn in 2025E, also roughly double its 2018 level, supported by expanded bank lending (about GEL 1.6bn) and government agro-credit programs.

Consumption of key agricultural products reached GEL 6.4bn in 2025, with imports of GEL 2.8bn and exports of GEL 3.0bn. Georgia relies on imports for meat, dairy and vegetables (meat self-sufficiency only about 39%, fish about 13%), while fruits, nuts and grape-based alcohol are largely exported. Exports (US$1.1bn) are concentrated in wine (24%), brandy (24%) and nuts (15%), and remain heavily CIS-facing (about 70% to CIS; wine 64% and fruits 74% to Russia).

The sector's core structural feature is low corporatization: a large share of output comes from low-productivity households (businesses are only about 28% of selected-product output and about 13% of primary production), and land is highly fragmented (73% of farms are under 1ha). Yields lag regional and world peers across fruits, cereals and vegetables. Blueberries are a fast-growing export segment, with production up 8.5x over 2019-23 to about 4mn kg, around 2,000ha planted and yields of 14.5 ton/ha (7th globally), though more than 90% of exports go to Russia.

Agriculture.outlook:
Galt & Taggart's Agricultural Development Index (productivity, price stability and investment sub-indices) and forecasts point to a sector with substantial headroom: the food-product market is projected to reach GEL 30bn by 2030, and consumption of cheese, fish, poultry and pork could reach about GEL 3bn by 2030, leaving room to expand local production by an additional roughly GEL 1bn through import substitution.

Real agricultural growth is expected to roughly double under a business-expansion scenario versus the baseline. The central market trajectory is a transition from household to corporatized, technology-enabled production, supported by lending, government programs, cold-storage build-out and export diversification beyond CIS. Blueberries illustrate both the upside and the diversification challenge, as production capacity is set to far exceed Russian demand by 2027, making new EU markets (Germany, Netherlands, UK, Poland) increasingly important.

Hospitality.headline: Tourism back in high gear: 5.3mn visitor trips and US$3.6bn travel income in 9M2025, with branded-hotel occupancy averaging 62%.
Hospitality.summary:
Georgia's tourism recovery continued through 2025. International visitor trips rose 5.6% y/y to 5.3mn in 9M2025, while tourist arrivals (excluding same-day trips) grew 7.9% y/y to 4.3mn. Income from foreign travel reached US$3.6bn in 9M2025, up 5.1% y/y. Same-day trips declined about 3%, reflecting a quality-over-quantity shift. Russia (23% of visits), Turkey (18%) and Armenia (14%) remained the top source markets, while the EU and UK overtook Israel and Azerbaijan with a 7.4% share as direct flights expanded.

Hotel performance strengthened. Occupancy in large branded hotels averaged 62% in 9M2025 (+5ppts y/y), with September running 11ppts above the prior year; ADR averaged US$134, slightly below 2024. Spending data show non-residents outspending residents roughly 3x on accommodation and about 4x at restaurants.

The Ajara/Batumi market is bifurcated: Middle Eastern visitors (notably from Israel and Saudi Arabia) drive hotel demand, while Russian and Central Asian tourists fuel the apartment and short-term-rental market. Batumi nights spent by international tourists rose 57.5% over 2019-24, branded hotel room supply in Batumi roughly doubled to about 4,079 rooms over 2019-24 (14.3% CAGR), and short-term rental apartments are projected to roughly double to about 35,000-40,000 by 2029.

Hospitality.outlook:
Galt & Taggart frames tourism as 'shifting into high gear,' with arrivals and receipts both growing and a healthier high-spending mix lifting hotel KPIs. Occupancy and revenues in Batumi and Tbilisi improved in 2025, driven by Middle Eastern and Russian/EU demand respectively.

The medium-term tension is supply and competition: Batumi's rapid build-out of branded rooms and short-term rental apartments risks oversupply unless arrivals keep climbing or length of stay improves, while regional casino legalization (UAE, Azerbaijan) could pressure a key demand pillar. Commonly cited mitigants include promoting long-stay tourism (digital nomads, medical and wellness) and public-private coordination.
